analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover at least 48 hours of hospital care after childbirth, 96 after a C-section.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in either committee it was sent to, and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997; Congress passed a similar hospital-stay guarantee later that same year.
analysis.plain_summary: The MOMS Act would have stopped insurers from pushing mothers and newborns out of the hospital within hours of birth. Any plan covering maternity care would have to pay for at least 48 hours in the hospital after a vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean, with no pre-approval required. Mothers who chose to go home early, together with their doctor, would have been entitled to a nurse or other provider visit at home within 72 hours. The bill also barred insurers from paying mothers to leave early or cutting payments to doctors who followed the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Mothers and newborns with maternity coverage, who would no longer face 'drive-through deliveries' where insurers limit the hospital stay to 24 hours or less. Doctors and nurses who care for them would be protected from reimbursement cuts for keeping mothers in the hospital.

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans covering maternity benefits to pay for a minimum 48-hour hospital stay after a vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean, without requiring the attending provider to get prior authorization from the plan [S3].

Lets a mother leave earlier only if her attending provider decides, in consultation with her, that early discharge is appropriate — and then the plan must cover timely follow-up care, with a home visit option, within 72 hours of discharge [S3].

Bars insurers from denying or dropping a mother's coverage for invoking these rights, from paying mothers rebates to leave the hospital early, and from penalizing or offering incentives to providers to discharge early [S3].
Leaves state laws with stronger protections in place, so the federal floor would not weaken states that already required longer stays [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who fund employee health plans would bear the added cost of longer covered hospital stays, generally passed along through higher premiums. Hospitals and obstetric providers would deliver more covered inpatient care.

drawbacks.text: The mandate adds to health costs: insurers and self-insured employers would pay for more inpatient days, a cost that generally flows into higher premiums and benefits for workers and plan buyers [S3].

Critics of minimum-stay mandates argue that a fixed hours standard substitutes a rule for medical judgment and adds routine hospital days that carry infection risk, though the bill responds by allowing early discharge with the provider's and mother's agreement plus mandatory follow-up care [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to mothers and newborns is substantial and targeted: an extra day or two in the hospital around childbirth, at a moment when complications are common, with a home-visit option for those who prefer to leave early. The cost is real but modest and spread across all premium payers rather than concentrated on anyone. This was the design Congress substantially copied later in 1996 when it passed a similar stay guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to their health and employment subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell introduced the bill on May 10, 1996, and it was referred to the Commerce Committee and the Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee [S5].
Five House Democrats cosponsored it; no Republican cosponsors appear on the record [S4].

On May 15 it went to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and on June 7 to the Economic and Educational Opportunities Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations; neither subcommittee acted [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

Later in the same year, Congress separately enacted the Newborns' and Mothers' Health Protection Act, which imposed a similar 48-hour/96-hour stay requirement on group health plans — so mothers eventually received this protection by a different route.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For the bill itself, insurers and employers escaped the mandate. But mothers and newborns did not lose in the end: a nearly identical hospital-stay guarantee was enacted later in 1996, so the practical protection became law by another route.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, until a similar law passed later in 1996

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the MOMS Act and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: Rep. Thomas Bliley
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee or scheduled it for consideration after referral.

against.name: House subcommittees on Health and Environment and Employer-Employee Relations
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in May and June 1996 and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only Democratic support — Dingell and five Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican cosponsors and no votes that would reveal broader partisan positions [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have forced plans covering maternity care to pay for guaranteed minimum hospital stays and barred the cost-saving tools insurers used at the time — early-discharge rebates to mothers and incentives to providers. Its death left insurers free of this mandate from this bill.
Employee health benefit plans were directly covered and would have absorbed the cost of longer stays under ERISA-style enforcement, typically passed on to employees as higher premiums.
More covered inpatient days and protection from reimbursement cuts for following the minimum-stay rules; their interest ran alongside mothers' in this bill.
